Primary subject: an illusionistic architectural ceiling PAINTING on an approximately FLAT, very shallow solid plastered wooden temporary ceiling cover above the crossing of an early-1700s Baroque church in Ljubljana, around 1703. Photograph the actual painted material from beneath. The main subject is the solid painted surface: the sky and every apparently receding architectural feature are pigment on the same nearly flat covered surface. There is no physical open roof, real dome, deep concave vault, tall drum, lantern, or opening behind the central image. The photograph must visibly distinguish the shallow painted material from the illusion it carries. This is an original fictional interpretation, with no claim of precisely measured original geometry.
Painting: invent a wholly new restrained Baroque perspective design, with an oval-looking ring of painted balustrades, painted pilasters converging toward a pale painted sky, and light painted clouds. These architectural forms are two-dimensional brushwork with painted shadows, NOT masonry projecting into real depth. No saints, portraits, named figures, copied iconography or existing artwork composition. No people or painted human figures are needed.
Physical surface: a broad, thin, gently worn plastered timber cover closes the entire crossing. Keep its whole approximately flat perimeter visible, with a narrow plain plaster strip and a shallow panel joint continuing across one peripheral section of the painting. Fine brushwork, lime-plaster grain and a faint substrate seam continue over the painted architectural illusion and sky. There must be no genuine hole or real window in this central cover. Avoid a deep spherical or bowl-shaped surface: its physical surface remains nearly flat or very shallow from edge to center.
Surroundings: only a narrow margin of real pale plaster Baroque supporting arches and pilasters on the sides and bottom, very modest simple moulding, visibly unfinished blank plaster areas, sparse early decoration. This is before the church's later completed nave frescoes and furnishings. No lavish later marble cladding or gilding, no modern 1841 dome, no exact recreation of the current cathedral. No benches, visitors, scaffolding, chandeliers, electric lamps or wiring.
Composition: wide upward-and-slightly-forward view from near the nave crossing, camera a little off the ideal perspective point so the shallow painted cover is legible as material. Painted ceiling occupies about three quarters of the frame; a small margin of real supporting arches provides architectural scale. The entire image uses the native 3:2 canvas without cropping or borders. Show enough perimeter and subtle seam to make the trompe-l'oeil clear even in a 480-pixel-wide preview.
Medium and light: convincing camera-captured photograph of painted plaster and historic architecture, natural soft lateral window daylight, faint warm reflected candle light from below, modest exposure. Muted chalky ivory, warm stone, subdued ochre and quiet pale blue pigment. Realistic matte plaster, pigment and wood-supported panel materials, small material irregularities, ordinary camera detail. No glowing heavenly portal, no HDR, no oversaturated color, no cinematic grading, no glossy CGI or fantasy spectacle.
Avoid: actual open real dome or roof, deep physical space above the ceiling cover, modern architecture, actual Quaglio or Langus panels, museum artefact replicas, copied composition, real-person likenesses, recognizable faces, people, words, numerals, Latin inscriptions, readable markings, signs, logos, watermark, captions, image frames or borders.
